definition: Roof overlay installation applies a new layer of asphalt shingles directly over one existing sound shingle layer without removing the old covering. It adds a second layer rather than stripping the roof to the deck, so it skips the tear-off labor and disposal, and is limited to a roof carrying no more than one existing layer over a smooth, dry, sound deck (the recover ARMA defines as installing an additional roof covering on an existing roof covering). It is only code-compliant in New Jersey under the N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 and IRC R908.3.1.1 eligibility limits.

costRanges.range: Roughly 20-25% less than a full tear-off, commonly ~$2,000-$5,000 cheaper for a typical home (national figure; an overlay skips the tear-off labor and disposal)
Added cost when loose, curled, or missing shingles need nailing down or replacing to create the smooth surface the recover requires (no flat figure sourced; a per-condition add-on)
costRanges.source: GAF Technical Bulletin TAB-R-145 and Owens Corning installation instructions (per gold)

costRanges.range: A future re-roof over two layers removes both layers at higher tear-off and disposal cost (no flat figure sourced)
costRanges.source: IRC Section R908.3.1.1 and Angi (per gold)

signs: One existing asphalt-shingle layer over a sound, dry, smooth deck qualifies a roof for an overlay, because GAF Technical Bulletin TAB-R-145 permits a recover only where one roof is in place and the surface lies smooth, and a complete tear-off is necessary where more than one roof is in place.

A deck that is water-soaked, rotted, spongy, or sagging disqualifies an overlay and requires a tear-off, because N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 bars a recover over a deteriorated deck and the IRC reroofing provisions, Section R908, prohibit roofing over an unsound base, per the NJ Uniform Construction Code and InterNACHI.

A roof already carrying two or more shingle layers disqualifies an overlay, because N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 and IRC Section R908.3.1.1 cap a roof at two total layers and prohibit a third layer, per the NJ Uniform Construction Code.

A wood shake, slate, clay, cement, or asbestos-cement tile covering disqualifies an overlay, because N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 bars a recover over those coverings, listing wood shake expressly, per the NJ Rehabilitation Subcode.

Curled, distorted, or uneven existing shingles that do not lie flat disqualify an overlay, because asphalt shingles take the shape of the surface beneath and telegraph the old profile, so a smooth substrate is required, per Owens Corning installation instructions and GAF Technical Bulletin TAB-R-145.

A roof past the asphalt service life of 20 years for 3-tab or 30 years for architectural favors a tear-off over an overlay, because an overlay traps heat that cuts the new shingles' life by roughly 20-30%, per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart and a national Angi industry estimate.

Structural sagging across the ridge or truss lines, or a deck revealing rotted or warped wood or gaps wider than 1/4 inch, makes a recover inappropriate and points to a tear-off, because those conditions show the base is no longer adequate, per ARMA.
selectionCriteria: Confirm the contractor holds active New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor registration, the credential the NJ Division of Consumer Affairs requires of every NJ roofing contractor under N.J.S.A. 56:8-136, with the 13VH registration number printed on the contract and advertising per N.J.S.A. 56:8-144 (it is a registration, not a license; NJ issues no roofing license).
Require proof of at least $500,000 per occurrence commercial general liability coverage under N.J.S.A. 56:8-142, verified directly on a current Certificate of Insurance.
Insist on a written contract for any project over $500 under N.J.A.C. 13:45A-16.2, with an itemized written estimate setting scope, labor, materials, and timeline before work begins.

Require a documented overlay eligibility inspection that checks the roof against the three N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 bar conditions (water-soaked or deteriorated deck; wood shake, slate, clay, cement, or asbestos-cement tile covering; two or more existing layers) and confirms one sound asphalt layer over a smooth, dry deck before quoting a recover.

Require the written estimate to state the overlay trade-offs against a tear-off in writing (a hidden deck, a roughly 20-30% shorter shingle life, a telegraphed profile, and added dead load) rather than presenting an overlay as equal to a tear-off.
Ask for local Essex County references and a documented assessment with photos, not a verbal quote.

On any storm- or fire-related claim, confirm the contractor stays in its lawful role: it documents the damage and meets the insurer's adjuster on site, while the homeowner or a licensed public adjuster negotiates the claim under N.J.S.A. 17:22B; reject any offer to waive or absorb the deductible, guarantee approval, or provide a 'free roof.'

technicalFacts.fact: A roof overlay (recover) is the installation of an additional roof covering over an existing roof covering, while a full replacement (tear-off) removes the existing covering, repairs any damaged substrate, and installs a new covering.

A roof overlay is not allowed in New Jersey where the deck is water-soaked or deteriorated, where the existing covering is wood shake, slate, clay, cement, or asbestos-cement tile, or where two or more shingle layers already exist; the NJ subcode lists wood shake expressly, unlike the model IRC.
technicalFacts.source: N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 (NJ Rehabilitation Subcode); IRC Section R908.3.1.1

technicalFacts.fact: A roof is capped at two total layers; no third layer is permitted, and a future re-roof over two layers requires tearing off both at higher cost.

An overlay traps heat between the layers that runs the new shingles hotter than designed and cuts service life by roughly 20-30%, so a 30-year architectural shingle delivers closer to 20-24 years over an overlay; the 3-tab 20-year and architectural 30-year baselines come from the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart.
technicalFacts.source: Angi (20-30% reduction, national industry estimate); InterNACHI (life-expectancy chart)

technicalFacts.fact: An overlay telegraphs the old shingle profile because asphalt shingles seal and lie against the surface beneath and take its shape, so a smooth substrate is required for a sound install.
technicalFacts.source: Owens Corning Three-Tab Installation Instructions; GAF Technical Bulletin TAB-R-145

technicalFacts.fact: A tear-off lets the roofer inspect and repair the deck; a recover hides it, so a recover hides any deck rot a tear-off catches and repairs and adds dead load across the deck, rafters, and supporting walls (roughly 2 to 4.5 lb per square foot for one asphalt layer).
technicalFacts.source: ARMA; InterNACHI; Dumpsters.com/Sourgum and Angi (dead-load range)

technicalFacts.fact: GAF shingles can be installed over an existing roof only where one roof is in place, the surface is smooth, loose or protruding nails are removed, loose or curled shingles are nailed down, and missing shingles are replaced; the GAF Shingle & Accessory Limited Warranty applies only if shingles are applied in strict accordance with GAF's printed application instructions, so a non-conforming recover can fall outside warranty coverage.
technicalFacts.source: GAF Technical Bulletin TAB-R-145; GAF Shingle & Accessory Limited Warranty

technicalFacts.fact: For a detached one- and two-family dwelling, repair or replacement of the roof covering counts as ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and requires no construction permit, no inspection, and no notice to the construction official; the exemption does not authorize a non-compliant recover.

A roof warranty has two parts: the manufacturer's material warranty (factory defects, preserved when installed to manufacturer specification per Owens Corning warranty guidance) and the contractor's written workmanship warranty on the labor.
technicalFacts.source: Owens Corning warranty guidance; GAF Shingle & Accessory Limited Warranty

defabToKill.issue: 'In Essex County's climate, asphalt shingles typically last 18-22 years.' and 'A single-layer roof at 15-20 years old' — invented local lifespan numbers with no source.
defabToKill.fix: Use the sourced baselines: 3-tab ~20 years and architectural ~30 years per the InterNACHI life-expectancy chart; note an overlay cuts new-shingle life by roughly 20-30% per a national Angi industry estimate. Do not assert an Essex-specific lifespan.

defabToKill.issue: 'original wood shingle layers sometimes lurk beneath asphalt, disqualifying overlay' framed loosely; and 'Moss or algae growth covering more than 25% of the roof surface' as a disqualifier — the 25% moss threshold is unsourced/invented.
defabToKill.fix: Ground the wood-shake disqualifier in N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4, which bars a recover over wood shake, slate, clay, cement, or asbestos-cement tile and lists wood shake expressly. Drop the invented 25% moss threshold; the real disqualifiers are the three N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 bar conditions plus curled/distorted shingles that won't lie flat (Owens Corning/GAF) and a soft/spongy/sagging deck (ARMA/IRC R908).

defabToKill.issue: Local hyper-specifics presented as fact: 'ice dams form along north-facing eaves in Cedar Grove and West Orange', 'Montclair and Glen Ridge homes surrounded by mature tree canopy', 'Maplewood and South Orange, where homes from the 1920s-1940s dominate.' Unsourced geographic/climate claims and a fabricated housing-stock statistic.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the invented neighborhood-level climate and housing-age assertions. Keep the code-grounded eligibility logic (layer count, deck condition, covering type) which applies across Essex County without fabricated local statistics.

defabToKill.issue: 'A standard asphalt shingle overlay on a typical Essex County home runs $6,500-$11,000, compared to $8,500-$15,000 for a tear-off replacement.' Invented flat whole-job totals; no NJ/Essex overlay-vs-tear-off total is sourced anywhere in the gold or fact pack.
defabToKill.fix: Replace with the sourced delta: an overlay runs roughly 20-25% less than a full tear-off, commonly ~$2,000-$5,000 cheaper for a typical home (national figure per HomeGuide and Angi). For per-unit pricing use NJ architectural asphalt $6.50-$11.00/sq ft and 3-tab $5.50-$9.50/sq ft installed per Josten Roofing NJ pricing. State there is NO sourced whole-job NJ overlay total.

defabToKill.issue: 'no dumpster rental ($400-$600 savings), and no disposal fees ($300-$500 savings)' — invented itemized savings figures.
defabToKill.fix: Frame the savings qualitatively/nationally: an overlay skips the tear-off labor and disposal, which is what produces the ~20-25% / ~$2,000-$5,000 saving (HomeGuide/Angi, national). Do not assert exact NJ dumpster or disposal dollar amounts.

defabToKill.issue: 'GAF's Golden Pledge warranty, for instance, is not available on overlay projects. CertainTeed similarly limits their SureStart Plus coverage' — named premium-warranty program claims used as NQR-relevant fact, and a CertainTeed program detail not in the gold.
defabToKill.fix: Explain warranty honestly as two parts: the manufacturer's material warranty (factory defects, preserved only when shingles install in strict accordance with GAF's printed application instructions over one existing layer and a smooth deck per GAF TAB-R-145 / Owens Corning instructions) and the contractor's written workmanship warranty on labor. A recover outside those printed conditions can fall outside warranty coverage, per GAF. Do not invoke Golden Pledge / SureStart Plus program names.

defabToKill.issue: 'overlay roofs averaging 15-18 years in the northeast versus 20-25 years for tear-off installations' — invented regional lifespan figures; and 'a $500 deck repair... can become a $5,000 emergency repair' — invented deck-repair dollar figures.
defabToKill.fix: Use the sourced lifespan: an overlay cuts new-shingle service life by roughly 20-30% (national Angi industry estimate), so a 30-year architectural shingle delivers closer to 20-24 years over an overlay (InterNACHI baselines). For the hidden-deck point, state qualitatively that a recover hides deck rot a tear-off catches and repairs (ARMA/InterNACHI); drop the invented $500 and $5,000 figures.

defabToKill.issue: 'particularly through Essex County's freeze-thaw cycles and hurricane season' — unsourced climate framing used to push the sale.
defabToKill.fix: Remove the unsourced climate/hurricane framing. Keep the factual point that delaying a needed reroof lets the existing roof keep failing, without inventing climate drivers.

defabToKill.issue: 'Your contractor will pull a building permit from your Essex County municipality. Even though overlay is less invasive than tear-off, NJ code requires permits for any re-roofing project. Inspection requirements vary by town: Newark requires post-installation inspection...' — directly contradicts the code: a 1-2 family roof covering is ordinary maintenance needing NO permit, and the per-town inspection detail is invented.
defabToKill.fix: State the actual rule: repair or replacement (including overlay) of the roof covering on a detached one- and two-family dwelling is ordinary maintenance under N.J.A.C. 5:23-2.7 and requires no construction permit, no inspection, and no notice to the construction official; the exemption does not authorize a non-compliant recover, which must still meet N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4. Do not assert a permit requirement or per-town inspection rules; do not state a permit-fee figure.

defabToKill.issue: 'adds ice-and-water shield along the first three feet of eave line as required by NJ code' — asserts a specific NJ code mandate not substantiated in the gold or fact pack.
defabToKill.fix: Do not cite a specific 'first three feet ice-and-water shield as required by NJ code' mandate that is not in the source set. Keep the substrate-prep and to-manufacturer-spec installation facts that ARE grounded (GAF TAB-R-145 / Owens Corning: nail down loose/curled shingles, remove protruding nails, replace missing shingles, smooth substrate).

defabToKill.issue: 'Most Essex County overlay projects complete in a single day for average-sized homes' and 'Standard 1-inch roofing nails... 1.5-inch or 1.75-inch nails are required' — invented timeline and unsourced nail-length specifications.
defabToKill.fix: Drop the unsourced single-day timeline claim and the specific nail-length figures (not in the gold/fact pack). Keep the grounded install logic: a smooth substrate is prepared and the second asphalt layer is installed to manufacturer specification, the install that keeps the GAF or Owens Corning limited warranty in force per GAF TAB-R-145 / Owens Corning instructions.

defabToKill.issue: Position-3 article is framed as a process/how-to walkthrough ('Pre-Installation Steps', 'The Overlay Installation Process', 'Post-Installation and Maintenance') rather than the broad decision overview the H1 calls for.
defabToKill.fix: Reframe to the decision the homeowner actually faces: an overlay is only legal on one sound asphalt layer over a smooth, dry, sound deck (N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 / IRC R908.3.1.1), it is NOT equal to a tear-off (it hides the deck, cuts shingle life ~20-30%, telegraphs the old profile, adds dead load), and it saves ~20-25% / ~$2,000-$5,000 (national) only because it skips tear-off and disposal. That trade-off is the core thing to understand.

parentDebtToAvoid: The gold commercial block carries 'Newark Quality Roofing installs and services Firestone, Carlisle, and Johns Manville membrane systems' — do NOT reproduce this membrane brand-roster line in the articles.

Do NOT present GAF / CertainTeed / Owens Corning as NQR certifications or partnerships (no Master Elite, SELECT ShingleMaster, Preferred, Golden Pledge, SureStart Plus); name them ONLY as external warranty/data/guidance sources.

The gold credentialsHighlight lists 'NJ HIC Licensed' — this is the known stale chip; use 'registered NJ HIC' / 'registered New Jersey Home Improvement Contractor', never 'licensed,' since NJ issues no roofing license.
Avoid any 'fully licensed NJ contractor' framing or invented volume ('hundreds of roofs/overlays'); NQR is a registered NJ HIC serving Essex County with no stated counts.

articleAngles.signs: An overlay fits only when one existing asphalt-shingle layer sits over a sound, dry, smooth deck (GAF TAB-R-145); it is barred where the deck is water-soaked or deteriorated, the covering is wood shake/slate/clay/cement/asbestos-cement tile, or two or more layers already exist (N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 / IRC R908.3.1.1). The position-1 directAnswer states those qualifying-and-disqualifying signs as the eligibility test.
articleAngles.costGuide: There is NO sourced whole-job NJ/Essex overlay total. The position-2 directAnswer states that an overlay runs roughly 20-25% less than a full tear-off, commonly ~$2,000-$5,000 cheaper for a typical home (national figure per HomeGuide and Angi), because it skips the tear-off labor and disposal; NJ per-unit pricing is architectural asphalt $6.50-$11.00/sq ft and 3-tab $5.50-$9.50/sq ft installed per Josten Roofing NJ pricing.
articleAngles.decision: The single most important thing to understand: an overlay is NOT equal to a tear-off. It is legal only on one sound asphalt layer over a smooth, dry deck (N.J.A.C. 5:23-6.4 / IRC R908.3.1.1 cap a roof at two layers), and the ~20-25% upfront saving comes with real trade-offs — it hides any deck rot a tear-off would catch and repair, traps heat that cuts the new shingles' life by roughly 20-30%, telegraphs the old profile, and adds dead load. The decision is whether those trade-offs are acceptable for a qualifying roof, not how the install is sequenced.
